notes.title: Introduction to Operating Systems
notes.body:
An operating system (OS) is the software layer that manages hardware resources and provides common services so programs can run safely and efficiently.

### What an OS does
- **Resource manager:** shares the CPU, memory, disks and devices between many programs.
- **Abstraction provider:** turns raw hardware into convenient abstractions such as processes, files, sockets and virtual memory.
- **Protection and isolation:** stops one program (or user) from reading or corrupting another's data.

### Types of operating systems
| Type | Idea | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Batch | Jobs run one after another with no interaction | Early mainframes |
| Multiprogramming | Several jobs in memory; CPU switches when one waits for I/O | Early UNIX |
| Time-sharing | Rapid switching gives each user the illusion of a dedicated machine | Linux, Windows |
| Real-time | Guarantees deadlines (hard or soft) | VxWorks, FreeRTOS |
| Distributed | Many machines appear as one system | Plan 9, cluster OSes |

### Kernel architectures
- **Monolithic kernel:** all services (file system, drivers, scheduler) run in kernel space. Fast, but a bug can crash everything. *Linux.*
- **Microkernel:** only the essentials (IPC, scheduling, memory) in the kernel; everything else runs as user-space servers. More robust, more message-passing overhead. *MINIX, QNX.*
- **Hybrid:** a pragmatic mix. *Windows NT, macOS (XNU).*

### Interview questions
**Q: What is the difference between multiprogramming and multitasking?**
Multiprogramming keeps several programs in memory to keep the CPU busy when one waits for I/O. Multitasking (time-sharing) adds frequent preemptive switching so interactive users all get responsive service.

**Q: Why do we need an OS at all?**
Without it every program would have to drive hardware directly and could interfere with every other program. The OS provides isolation, fair sharing and reusable abstractions.

notes.title: System Calls and Kernel vs User Mode
notes.body:
A system call is the controlled entry point a user program uses to ask the kernel to do something privileged, such as reading a file or creating a process.

### Dual-mode operation
The CPU has at least two privilege levels:
- **User mode:** restricted; cannot execute privileged instructions or touch hardware directly.
- **Kernel mode:** full access to hardware and all memory.

A mode bit in the CPU tracks the current mode. Switching to kernel mode only happens through a trap (system call), an interrupt, or an exception, so user code can never just "decide" to be privileged.

### How a system call works
1. The program calls a library wrapper, e.g. `read()` in libc.
2. The wrapper puts the system call number and arguments in registers.
3. It executes a trap instruction (`syscall` on x86-64).
4. The CPU switches to kernel mode and jumps to the kernel's handler.
5. The kernel validates arguments, does the work, and returns to user mode with a result.

### Categories
| Category | Examples (POSIX) |
|---|---|
| Process control | `fork`, `exec`, `exit`, `wait` |
| File management | `open`, `read`, `write`, `close` |
| Device management | `ioctl` |
| Information | `getpid`, `time` |
| Communication | `pipe`, `socket`, `mmap` |

### Interview questions
**Q: Why are system calls expensive compared to normal function calls?**
They involve a mode switch, saving and restoring registers, argument validation and often cache/TLB pollution. That is why buffered I/O batches many small writes into one `write()`.

**Q: What does `fork()` return?**
It returns twice: `0` in the child and the child's PID in the parent (or `-1` on failure).

notes.title: Processes and the Process Control Block
notes.body:
A process is a program in execution: the code plus its current state, including registers, memory, open files and scheduling information.

### Program vs process
A **program** is a passive file on disk. A **process** is an active instance of it. Running the same program twice creates two independent processes.

### Memory layout of a process
| Segment | Contents |
|---|---|
| Text | Compiled machine code (read-only) |
| Data | Initialised global and static variables |
| BSS | Uninitialised globals (zero-filled) |
| Heap | Dynamic allocations (`malloc`, `new`); grows upward |
| Stack | Function frames, local variables, return addresses; grows downward |

### Process Control Block (PCB)
The kernel keeps one PCB per process. It holds:
- Process ID and parent ID
- Process state (new, ready, running, waiting, terminated)
- Saved CPU registers and program counter
- Scheduling info (priority, queue pointers)
- Memory-management info (page table base, limits)
- Accounting info (CPU time used)
- I/O status (open file descriptors)

### Process creation in UNIX
`fork()` duplicates the caller; `exec()` replaces the child's memory image with a new program. Modern kernels use **copy-on-write**, so `fork()` doesn't copy memory until one side writes to it.

### Interview questions
**Q: What is a zombie process?**
A child that has exited but whose parent hasn't called `wait()` to read its exit status. Its PCB entry stays until the parent reaps it.

**Q: What is an orphan process?**
A child whose parent exited first. On UNIX it is adopted by `init` (PID 1), which reaps it.

notes.title: Process States and Context Switching
notes.body:
A process moves through a small set of states, and a context switch is how the CPU stops running one process and resumes another.

### The five-state model
- **New:** being created.
- **Ready:** waiting for the CPU.
- **Running:** executing on a CPU.
- **Waiting (blocked):** waiting for I/O or an event.
- **Terminated:** finished, awaiting cleanup.

Transitions: *Ready → Running* (dispatched by scheduler), *Running → Ready* (preempted, time slice over), *Running → Waiting* (I/O request), *Waiting → Ready* (I/O complete), *Running → Terminated* (exit).

### Context switch steps
1. Save the running process's registers and program counter into its PCB.
2. Update its state (ready or waiting) and move it to the right queue.
3. Pick the next process (scheduler).
4. Load its saved registers, switch the address space (page table base register), and resume.

### Why context switches cost time
- Pure overhead: no useful user work is done.
- Switching address spaces can flush the TLB.
- The new process starts with cold caches.

Thread switches within the same process are cheaper because the address space stays the same.

### Schedulers
- **Long-term:** decides which jobs are admitted into memory (degree of multiprogramming).
- **Short-term (CPU scheduler):** picks the next ready process; runs very often.
- **Medium-term:** swaps processes out of memory and back to control load.

### Interview questions
**Q: What triggers a context switch?**
A timer interrupt ending the time slice, a blocking system call, a higher-priority process becoming ready, or the process exiting.

notes.title: Threads and Multithreading
notes.body:
A thread is the smallest unit of CPU scheduling: it has its own stack and registers but shares code, heap and open files with other threads in the same process.

### Process vs thread
| | Process | Thread |
|---|---|---|
| Memory | Own address space | Shares the process's address space |
| Creation cost | High | Low |
| Context switch | Slower (address-space switch) | Faster |
| Communication | IPC (pipes, sockets, shared memory) | Shared variables |
| Failure | Crash is isolated | One bad thread can crash the whole process |

### Benefits of multithreading
- **Responsiveness:** a UI thread stays responsive while a worker thread does heavy work.
- **Resource sharing:** threads share data without IPC.
- **Economy:** cheaper to create and switch than processes.
- **Scalability:** threads can run in parallel on multiple cores.

### Threading models
- **Many-to-one:** many user threads on one kernel thread. A blocking call blocks all of them; no true parallelism.
- **One-to-one:** each user thread maps to a kernel thread. True parallelism; used by Linux and Windows.
- **Many-to-many:** multiplexes user threads over a pool of kernel threads (e.g. Go goroutines on OS threads).

### Concurrency vs parallelism
**Concurrency** is dealing with many tasks at once (interleaved); **parallelism** is doing many at the same instant on multiple cores.

### Interview questions
**Q: What breaks if two threads increment the same counter without a lock?**
`count++` is a read-modify-write. Both threads can read the same old value and write back the same new value, losing an update. This is a race condition.

**Q: What does a thread NOT share with its siblings?**
Its stack, registers, program counter and thread-local storage.

notes.title: CPU Scheduling Algorithms
notes.body:
CPU scheduling decides which ready process runs next, balancing throughput, waiting time, response time and fairness.

### Metrics
- **Turnaround time** = completion time − arrival time
- **Waiting time** = turnaround time − burst time
- **Response time** = first time on CPU − arrival time
- **Throughput** = processes completed per unit time

### The main algorithms
| Algorithm | Preemptive? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| FCFS | No | Simple; suffers the **convoy effect** (short jobs stuck behind a long one) |
| SJF | No | Optimal average waiting time, but needs burst lengths in advance |
| SRTF | Yes | Preemptive SJF; can starve long jobs |
| Priority | Either | Can starve low priority; fixed by **aging** |
| Round Robin | Yes | Fixed time quantum; good response time |
| Multilevel queue | Yes | Separate queues (e.g. foreground RR, background FCFS) |
| Multilevel feedback queue | Yes | Jobs move between queues based on behaviour; approximates SJF without knowing bursts |

### Worked example (Round Robin, quantum = 2)
Processes P1 (5), P2 (3), P3 (1), all arriving at 0.
Order: P1(0–2), P2(2–4), P3(4–5), P1(5–7), P2(7–8), P1(8–9).
Completion: P3 = 5, P2 = 8, P1 = 9. Average turnaround = (9 + 8 + 5) / 3 = 7.33.

### Choosing the quantum
Too large and RR becomes FCFS; too small and the CPU spends most of its time context switching. Rule of thumb: most CPU bursts should finish within one quantum.

### Interview questions
**Q: What is starvation and how is it solved?**
A process waits indefinitely because others are always preferred. **Aging** gradually raises the priority of waiting processes.

**Q: Which scheduler does Linux use?**
The Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS), replaced by EEVDF in Linux 6.6. Both aim to give each task a fair share of CPU time.

notes.title: Inter-Process Communication (IPC)
notes.body:
IPC is the set of mechanisms that let separate processes exchange data and coordinate, since they do not share memory by default.

### Two basic models
- **Shared memory:** processes map the same memory region. Very fast after setup, but they must synchronize access themselves.
- **Message passing:** the kernel copies messages between processes. Simpler and safer, but each message costs a system call.

### Common mechanisms
| Mechanism | Description | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Pipe | One-way byte stream between related processes | `ls | grep foo` |
| Named pipe (FIFO) | Pipe with a name in the file system; unrelated processes can use it | Simple local services |
| Message queue | Kernel-managed queue of typed messages | Producer/consumer |
| Shared memory | Common memory segment (`shmget`, `mmap`) | High-throughput data exchange |
| Semaphores | Counters for synchronization (often paired with shared memory) | Coordinating access |
| Signals | Asynchronous notifications (`SIGINT`, `SIGKILL`) | Interrupting, terminating |
| Sockets | Bidirectional communication, locally or across a network | Client/server |

### Producer-consumer with a bounded buffer
A classic IPC pattern: the producer writes items into a fixed-size buffer and the consumer removes them. The producer must wait when the buffer is full and the consumer when it is empty, usually coordinated with semaphores or condition variables.

### Interview questions
**Q: Which IPC mechanism is fastest and why?**
Shared memory, because after it's set up data moves without kernel copies. The trade-off is that you must handle synchronization yourself.

**Q: Can `SIGKILL` be caught?**
No. `SIGKILL` and `SIGSTOP` cannot be caught, blocked or ignored.

notes.title: Process Synchronization and the Critical Section Problem
notes.body:
Synchronization makes sure that concurrent processes or threads accessing shared data don't interfere, which keeps results correct regardless of timing.

### Race condition
A race condition happens when the outcome depends on the unpredictable order in which threads run. Example: two threads both doing `balance = balance + 100` can lose one deposit.

### The critical section
The **critical section** is the code that accesses shared data. Each process follows the pattern:
```
entry section      // ask for permission
  critical section // touch shared data
exit section       // release permission
remainder section
```

### Requirements for a correct solution
1. **Mutual exclusion:** at most one process is in its critical section at a time.
2. **Progress:** if nobody is in the critical section, the choice of who enters next can't be postponed forever.
3. **Bounded waiting:** there's a limit on how many times others can enter before a waiting process gets its turn.

### Classical solutions
- **Peterson's algorithm:** a software solution for two processes using `flag[]` and `turn`. Correct in theory but can fail on modern CPUs that reorder memory operations unless memory barriers are used.
- **Hardware support:** atomic instructions such as **test-and-set** and **compare-and-swap (CAS)**, which build spinlocks and lock-free data structures.
- **OS primitives:** mutexes, semaphores, condition variables and monitors.

### Interview questions
**Q: What is a spinlock and when is it good?**
A lock that busy-waits in a loop until free. It's efficient on multi-core systems when the critical section is very short, because it avoids a context switch, and wasteful when held for long.

**Q: What is a lock-free algorithm?**
One that uses atomic operations such as CAS instead of locks, so some thread always makes progress even if others are paused.

notes.title: Mutex, Semaphores and Monitors
notes.body:
Mutexes, semaphores and monitors are the standard tools the OS and languages provide for enforcing mutual exclusion and coordinating threads.

### Mutex
A mutex is a lock with an owner: only the thread that locked it may unlock it. It provides mutual exclusion for a critical section.
```
lock(m)
  // critical section
unlock(m)
```

### Semaphore
A semaphore is an integer counter with two atomic operations:
- `wait()` / `P()`: decrement; if the value becomes negative, block.
- `signal()` / `V()`: increment; wake a waiting thread if any.

Types:
- **Binary semaphore** (0 or 1): similar to a mutex, but with no ownership.
- **Counting semaphore:** limits access to N identical resources, e.g. a pool of 5 database connections.

### Mutex vs semaphore
| | Mutex | Semaphore |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Mutual exclusion | Signalling and resource counting |
| Ownership | Yes: only the owner unlocks | No: any thread can signal |
| Values | Locked / unlocked | 0 to N |

### Condition variables and monitors
A **condition variable** lets a thread wait until some condition is true (`wait`, `signal`, `broadcast`). It is always used with a mutex and in a `while` loop, because of spurious wake-ups.

A **monitor** is a language construct that bundles shared data with the procedures that operate on it, guaranteeing that only one thread is inside at a time. Java's `synchronized` methods with `wait()`/`notify()` are monitors.

### Interview questions
**Q: Why must condition waits use a `while` loop instead of `if`?**
A woken thread might find the condition false again: another thread may have consumed the item first, or the wake-up may be spurious. Re-checking in a loop is always correct.

**Q: What is priority inversion?**
A high-priority task waits for a lock held by a low-priority task, which is itself preempted by a medium-priority task. **Priority inheritance** temporarily raises the lock holder's priority. This bug famously affected the Mars Pathfinder rover.

notes.title: Classic Synchronization Problems
notes.body:
Three textbook problems (bounded buffer, readers-writers and dining philosophers) capture most real-world synchronization patterns and are common interview topics.

### 1. Bounded buffer (producer-consumer)
Shared buffer of size N. Semaphores: `mutex = 1`, `empty = N`, `full = 0`.
```
Producer:                Consumer:
  wait(empty)              wait(full)
  wait(mutex)              wait(mutex)
  add item                 remove item
  signal(mutex)            signal(mutex)
  signal(full)             signal(empty)
```
Swapping the order of `wait(empty)` and `wait(mutex)` can deadlock: the producer holds the mutex while waiting for space that the consumer can never free.

### 2. Readers-writers
Many readers may read at once, but a writer needs exclusive access.
- **First readers-writers problem:** readers get priority; writers can starve.
- **Second readers-writers problem:** writers get priority; readers can starve.
- Real systems use **read-write locks** (`pthread_rwlock`, `ReentrantReadWriteLock`), often with fairness policies.

### 3. Dining philosophers
Five philosophers sit around a table with one chopstick between each pair. Each needs both neighbours' chopsticks to eat. If all pick up their left chopstick at once, they deadlock.

Fixes:
- **Resource ordering:** always pick up the lower-numbered chopstick first (breaks circular wait).
- Allow at most four philosophers at the table at a time.
- Pick up both chopsticks only if both are free (inside a monitor).
- Asymmetry: odd philosophers pick left first, even ones pick right first.

### Interview questions
**Q: How do you avoid starvation in readers-writers?**
Use a fair lock that queues requests in arrival order, or let a waiting writer block new readers from entering.

**Q: What general lesson does dining philosophers teach?**
Acquiring multiple locks in inconsistent order causes deadlock; a global lock ordering is the simplest prevention.

notes.title: Deadlocks
notes.body:
A deadlock is a state where a set of processes are each waiting for a resource held by another process in the set, so none of them can ever proceed.

### The four Coffman conditions
A deadlock can occur only if **all four** hold at the same time:
1. **Mutual exclusion:** a resource can be held by only one process at a time.
2. **Hold and wait:** a process holds resources while waiting for more.
3. **No preemption:** resources cannot be taken away; they're released voluntarily.
4. **Circular wait:** a cycle P1 → P2 → … → P1, where each waits for the next.

### Handling strategies
| Strategy | Idea | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Prevention | Break one of the four conditions (e.g. global lock ordering) | Can lower resource utilisation |
| Avoidance | Only grant requests that keep the system in a *safe state* (Banker's algorithm) | Needs maximum demands in advance |
| Detection and recovery | Let deadlocks happen, detect cycles, then kill or roll back processes | Detection overhead plus lost work |
| Ignore (ostrich) | Assume deadlocks are rare | Used by most general-purpose OSes |

### Banker's algorithm (avoidance)
For each request, the OS pretends to grant it and checks whether there is still some order in which every process can finish with the available resources (a **safe sequence**). If yes, it grants the request; otherwise the process waits.

### Detection
With single-instance resources, build a **wait-for graph** and look for a cycle. With multiple instances, use a Banker's-like detection algorithm.

### Deadlock vs livelock vs starvation
- **Deadlock:** everyone is blocked forever.
- **Livelock:** processes keep changing state in response to each other but make no progress (two people stepping aside in a corridor).
- **Starvation:** one process waits indefinitely while others proceed.

### Interview questions
**Q: What is the most practical way to prevent deadlocks in application code?**
Acquire locks in a consistent global order, hold them briefly, and use timeouts (`tryLock`) so threads back off instead of waiting forever.

notes.title: Memory Management Basics
notes.body:
Memory management decides where each process lives in RAM, translates the addresses programs use into physical addresses, and protects processes from one another.

### Logical vs physical addresses
Programs use **logical (virtual) addresses**. The **Memory Management Unit (MMU)** translates them to **physical addresses** at run time. The simplest scheme adds a base register and checks a limit register.

### Address binding
Addresses can be bound at compile time, load time or execution time. Modern systems bind at execution time, which allows processes to move in memory.

### Contiguous allocation
Each process gets one contiguous block.
- **Fixed partitions:** memory is split into fixed-size slots, causing internal fragmentation.
- **Variable partitions:** blocks are sized to fit, causing external fragmentation.

Placement strategies for a request:
| Strategy | Picks | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| First fit | The first hole large enough | Fast |
| Best fit | The smallest hole large enough | Leaves tiny unusable holes |
| Worst fit | The largest hole | Leaves big holes, but generally performs worst |

### Fragmentation
- **Internal fragmentation:** wasted space *inside* an allocated block (asked for 18 KB, got 20 KB).
- **External fragmentation:** enough total free memory exists, but it is split into non-contiguous holes.
- **Compaction** shuffles processes together to remove external fragmentation, but it is expensive.

### Swapping
A process can be temporarily moved out to disk (swapped out) and brought back later, letting the system run more processes than fit in RAM.

### Interview questions
**Q: How do paging and segmentation relate to fragmentation?**
Paging eliminates external fragmentation, at the cost of some internal fragmentation in the last page. Segmentation avoids internal fragmentation but suffers from external fragmentation.

notes.title: Paging and Page Tables
notes.body:
Paging splits virtual memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into equal-size frames, so a process's memory no longer needs to be contiguous.

### How translation works
A virtual address is split into a **page number (p)** and an **offset (d)**. The page table maps `p` to a frame number `f`, and the physical address is `f × page_size + d`.

Example: 4 KB pages and a 32-bit address give 12 offset bits and 20 page-number bits, so up to about 1 million page-table entries per process.

### Page table entry (PTE) bits
- **Valid/present:** the page is in memory.
- **Frame number**
- **Protection:** read / write / execute.
- **Dirty:** the page has been modified and must be written back before eviction.
- **Referenced (accessed):** used by page-replacement algorithms.

### Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)
Looking up the page table in memory doubles memory accesses. The **TLB** is a small, fast cache of recent translations.
- **TLB hit:** translation in about 1 cycle.
- **TLB miss:** walk the page table, then cache the result.

**Effective access time** = hit ratio × (TLB + memory) + (1 − hit ratio) × (TLB + 2 × memory)

### Making page tables smaller
- **Multi-level (hierarchical) page tables:** only allocate the parts of the table actually used. x86-64 uses 4 or 5 levels.
- **Inverted page table:** one entry per physical frame rather than per virtual page.
- **Hashed page tables:** common for address spaces larger than 32 bits.

### Interview questions
**Q: Why do larger pages reduce TLB misses but increase waste?**
Each TLB entry then covers more memory, so fewer entries are needed, but the unused tail of each page (internal fragmentation) grows. "Huge pages" (2 MB or 1 GB) help databases with large memory footprints.

**Q: What happens on a TLB miss versus a page fault?**
A TLB miss only means walking the page table, which is cheap. A page fault means the page isn't in RAM at all: the OS must load it from disk, which is very expensive.

notes.title: Segmentation
notes.body:
Segmentation divides a program's memory into variable-sized logical units, such as code, data, stack and heap, matching how programmers think about a program.

### How it works
A logical address is a pair **(segment number, offset)**. The **segment table** stores, for each segment, a **base** (start physical address) and a **limit** (length).
- If `offset < limit`, the physical address is `base + offset`.
- Otherwise the hardware raises a **segmentation fault**.

### Advantages
- Matches the program's logical structure.
- Protection and sharing per segment, e.g. a read-only shared code segment.
- No internal fragmentation, because segments are sized exactly.

### Disadvantages
- **External fragmentation**, because segments vary in size.
- Allocation is harder (first fit or best fit, plus compaction).

### Paging vs segmentation
| | Paging | Segmentation |
|---|---|---|
| Unit size | Fixed (pages) | Variable (segments) |
| Visible to programmer | No | Yes |
| Fragmentation | Internal | External |
| Address | Page number + offset | Segment number + offset |

### Segmented paging
Many systems combine both: each segment is itself paged. This keeps the logical view of segments while avoiding external fragmentation. Classic x86 used segmentation plus paging. x86-64 mostly flattens segmentation and relies on paging.

### Interview questions
**Q: Where does the term "segmentation fault" come from today?**
It originally meant accessing beyond a segment's limit. Today it generally means accessing memory your process isn't allowed to touch (an invalid or protected page), detected by the MMU.

notes.title: Virtual Memory and Demand Paging
notes.body:
Virtual memory lets each process use a large, private address space that can exceed physical RAM, by keeping only the pages that are actually in use in memory.

### Benefits
- Programs can be larger than physical memory.
- More processes fit in memory at once (higher multiprogramming).
- Isolation: each process has its own address space.
- Efficient `fork()` via copy-on-write, and memory-mapped files.

### Demand paging
Pages are loaded only when first accessed, not all at program start.

**Handling a page fault:**
1. The CPU references a page whose PTE is marked invalid, and traps to the OS.
2. The OS checks the reference is legal (if not, it kills the process with a segfault).
3. It finds a free frame, or evicts a page using page replacement.
4. It schedules a disk read of the page into the frame.
5. It updates the page table and marks the page valid.
6. It restarts the faulting instruction.

### Performance
**Effective access time** = (1 − p) × memory_access + p × page_fault_time.
A page fault (around 8 ms on disk) is about 100,000 times slower than a memory access (around 100 ns). So even a fault rate of 1 in 1,000 slows memory access by roughly 80 times. Keeping fault rates tiny is essential.

### Copy-on-write (COW)
After `fork()`, parent and child share pages marked read-only. Only when one of them writes does the OS copy that specific page. This makes `fork()` followed by `exec()` cheap.

### Interview questions
**Q: What is the difference between a minor and a major page fault?**
A minor fault is resolved without disk I/O (the page is already in memory, for example in the page cache or shared with another process). A major fault requires reading the page from disk.

notes.title: Page Replacement Algorithms
notes.body:
When a page fault occurs and no frame is free, a page replacement algorithm chooses which resident page to evict, aiming to minimise future faults.

### The algorithms
| Algorithm | Evicts | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| FIFO | The oldest loaded page | Simple; suffers **Belady's anomaly** |
| Optimal (OPT) | The page used furthest in the future | Lowest possible faults; impossible in practice, used as a benchmark |
| LRU | The least recently used page | Good approximation of OPT; costly to implement exactly |
| Clock (second chance) | FIFO, but skips pages whose reference bit is set (clearing it) | Practical LRU approximation used by real OSes |
| LFU / MFU | Least / most frequently used | Rarely used alone |

### Worked example (3 frames)
Reference string: `7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4`
- **FIFO:** 7, 0, 1 (3 faults) → 2 replaces 7 → 0 hit → 3 replaces 0 → 0 replaces 1 → 4 replaces 2. **7 faults.**
- **LRU:** 7, 0, 1 (3) → 2 replaces 7 → 0 hit → 3 replaces 1 → 0 hit → 4 replaces 2. **6 faults.**

### Belady's anomaly
With FIFO, adding more frames can *increase* the number of page faults. Example string: `1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5` gives 9 faults with 3 frames but 10 faults with 4. LRU and OPT are **stack algorithms** and never show this anomaly.

### Dirty pages
Evicting a clean page is free. A dirty page must first be written to disk, so algorithms prefer clean victims; the enhanced clock algorithm uses both the reference and the dirty bit.

### Interview questions
**Q: How would you implement an LRU cache in O(1)?**
Combine a hash map (key → node) with a doubly linked list ordered by recency. On access, move the node to the front; on eviction, remove from the back. (This is LeetCode 146.)

notes.title: Thrashing and the Working Set
notes.body:
Thrashing is when a system spends more time swapping pages in and out than doing useful work, because processes don't have enough frames for the pages they actively use.

### Why it happens
1. Too many processes compete for too little memory.
2. Each process keeps faulting, and the CPU sits idle waiting for disk.
3. The OS sees low CPU utilisation and admits *more* processes.
4. Faults increase further, and throughput collapses.

### Locality of reference
Programs tend to reuse a small set of pages for a while (**temporal locality**) and to access nearby addresses (**spatial locality**). The set of pages in active use is the program's **locality**.

### Working set model
The **working set** WS(t, Δ) is the set of pages referenced in the last Δ references.
- If the sum of all working sets exceeds the available frames, thrashing is likely.
- The OS fixes this by **suspending (swapping out) a whole process** to free its frames for the others.

### Page-fault frequency (PFF)
A more direct control loop:
- If a process's fault rate is above an upper threshold, give it more frames.
- If its fault rate is below a lower threshold, take frames away.
- If no free frames are left, suspend a process.

### Interview questions
**Q: How can you tell a machine is thrashing?**
High disk I/O and paging activity (for example `vmstat` showing high si/so), low CPU utilisation, and very poor responsiveness.

**Q: Does adding RAM always fix thrashing?**
It fixes thrashing caused by insufficient memory. If one process's working set is unbounded, for example because of a memory leak, it only delays the problem.

notes.title: File Systems and Allocation Methods
notes.body:
A file system organises data on storage into files and directories and decides how each file's blocks are placed on disk.

### File system building blocks
- **File:** a named collection of data, plus metadata (size, owner, permissions, timestamps).
- **Directory:** maps names to files. Structures range from single-level to tree and acyclic-graph (with links).
- **Inode (UNIX):** a per-file structure holding metadata and pointers to data blocks. The file name lives in the directory entry, *not* in the inode.

### Allocation methods
| Method | How | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| Contiguous | File occupies consecutive blocks | Fast sequential and random access | External fragmentation; hard to grow files |
| Linked | Each block points to the next | No external fragmentation | Slow random access; a lost pointer corrupts the file |
| Indexed | An index block lists all data blocks | Fast random access; no fragmentation | Index-block overhead |

The **FAT** file system is linked allocation with the pointers moved into a table. **UNIX inodes** use multi-level indexing: 12 direct pointers plus single, double and triple indirect blocks, so small files are fast and large files are still possible.

### Free-space management
Bitmaps (one bit per block), linked free lists, or grouping and counting schemes.

### Journaling
A **journaling file system** (ext4, NTFS, APFS) first writes intended metadata changes to a log. After a crash, the log is replayed instead of scanning the whole disk with `fsck`.

### Hard links vs soft links
- **Hard link:** another directory entry pointing to the same inode. It can't cross file systems, and the data survives until all links are removed.
- **Soft (symbolic) link:** a separate file containing a path. It can cross file systems, and breaks if the target is deleted.

### Interview questions
**Q: What happens when you delete a file that another process still has open?**
On UNIX the name is removed immediately, but the inode and data stay until the last open file descriptor is closed.

notes.title: Disk Scheduling
notes.body:
Disk scheduling orders pending I/O requests on a hard disk to reduce seek time, the time the read/write head spends moving between tracks.

### Disk access time
Access time = **seek time** (moving the arm) + **rotational latency** (waiting for the sector) + **transfer time**. Seek time usually dominates, which is what scheduling targets.

### Algorithms
| Algorithm | Behaviour | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| FCFS | In arrival order | Fair but lots of seeking |
| SSTF | Nearest request first | Low seek time; can starve far requests |
| SCAN (elevator) | Sweeps to one end, then reverses | No starvation; edge tracks wait longer |
| C-SCAN | Sweeps one way, jumps back to the start | More uniform wait times |
| LOOK / C-LOOK | Like SCAN / C-SCAN but turns at the last request | Avoids pointless travel to the edge |

### Worked example
Head at 53, requests: 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67 (tracks 0–199).
- **FCFS:** total head movement 640.
- **SSTF:** 53 → 65 → 67 → 37 → 14 → 98 → 122 → 124 → 183, total 236.
- **SCAN (moving toward 0):** 53 → 37 → 14 → 0 → 65 → 67 → 98 → 122 → 124 → 183, total 236.

### SSDs change the picture
SSDs have no moving parts, so seek time is gone. OS schedulers for SSDs focus on fairness and merging requests (for example Linux's `none`/`mq-deadline`). SSD-specific concerns include **wear levelling**, **TRIM**, and write amplification.

### RAID (often asked alongside)
- **RAID 0:** striping (speed, no redundancy).
- **RAID 1:** mirroring.
- **RAID 5:** striping with distributed parity (survives one disk failure).
- **RAID 10:** mirrored stripes.

### Interview questions
**Q: Why can SSTF cause starvation?**
If new requests keep arriving near the head, a far-away request can be postponed indefinitely.

notes.title: Interrupts, I/O and the Boot Process
notes.body:
Interrupts let hardware get the CPU's attention asynchronously, and the boot process is the sequence that takes a machine from power-on to a running operating system.

### Interrupts
An **interrupt** is a signal that makes the CPU pause its current work and run an **interrupt handler (ISR)**.
- **Hardware interrupts:** from devices (keyboard, NIC, timer, disk completion).
- **Software interrupts / traps:** system calls.
- **Exceptions:** divide-by-zero, page fault, invalid opcode.

The **interrupt vector table** maps each interrupt number to its handler. The **timer interrupt** is what makes preemptive multitasking possible.

### Ways to do I/O
| Method | How | When it's good |
|---|---|---|
| Programmed I/O (polling) | The CPU repeatedly checks a device status register | Very fast devices, or very short waits |
| Interrupt-driven I/O | The device interrupts the CPU when it's ready | Most devices |
| DMA | A DMA controller moves whole blocks directly between device and memory, then interrupts once | Bulk transfers (disk, network) |

### Buffering, caching and spooling
- **Buffering:** temporary storage to smooth out speed differences between devices.
- **Caching:** keeping copies of frequently used data in faster storage.
- **Spooling:** queueing output for a device that can serve only one job at a time, such as a printer.

### The boot process (typical PC)
1. Power on: the CPU starts executing firmware (BIOS or **UEFI**).
2. **POST**: the firmware tests hardware.
3. The firmware finds the bootloader (MBR, or the EFI system partition).
4. The **bootloader** (e.g. GRUB) loads the kernel and the initial RAM disk.
5. The kernel initialises memory management, drivers and the scheduler, then mounts the root file system.
6. The kernel starts the first user process (`init` / `systemd`, PID 1), which starts services and the login screen.

### Interview questions
**Q: Why use DMA instead of interrupts for every byte?**
Interrupting the CPU per byte would overwhelm it at high data rates. DMA transfers a whole block and interrupts once at the end.
